lessons.title: Tissue in the wrong place, behaving badly
lessons.opening: You've spent years being told that period pain is just part of being a woman, and part of you started to believe it. Underneath, you kept wondering what was actually happening inside your body.

The guideline grades its recommendations for the clinical, imaging and surgical evaluation of endometriosis by strength and evidence quality, and adds ungraded good-practice points where evidence is inadequate or missing. The recommendations apply to adolescents as well as adults unless stated otherwise, though the adolescent guidance leans on data extrapolated from adults and on expert consensus (ACOG clinical practice guideline).Read the study on PubMed →[13]ESHRE guideline: endometriosis.Hum Reprod Open 2022 · PMID 35350465Laparoscopy and histology are no longer the unchallenged gold standard for diagnosing endometriosis — one of the notable shifts in this guideline's 109 recommendations spanning diagnosis, pain and infertility treatment, recurrence, asymptomatic and extrapelvic disease, adolescents, postmenopausal patients, prevention, and cancer association. What it actually is

Every month, the lining of your uterus (the endometrium) thickens and then sheds during your period. In endometriosis, tissue that looks and behaves like that lining ends up outside the uterus — on the ovaries, on the ligaments that hold the uterus in place, on the bladder, the bowel, the lining of the pelvis. Each month, that tissue still tries to bleed[1]Diagnosis of Endometriosis.Obstet Gynecol 2026 · PMID 41712950Clinical diagnosis is enough to start treating endometriosis - laparoscopy is no longer required first. The guideline grades its recommendations for the clinical, imaging and surgical evaluation of endometriosis by strength and evidence quality, and adds ungraded good-practice points where evidence is inadequate or missing. The recommendations apply to adolescents as well as adults unless stated otherwise, though the adolescent guidance leans on data extrapolated from adults and on expert consensus (ACOG clinical practice guideline).Read the study on PubMed →. But it has nowhere to go.

That trapped bleeding causes inflammation, scarring (called adhesions), and over time, deeply sensitized pain pathways. Endometriosis is not a disease of unusually heavy or painful periods alone — it is an estrogen-driven, inflammatory condition that grows and changes over years if it is not treated[2]Laparoscopic surgery for endometriosis.Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020 · PMID 33095458Laparoscopic treatment of endometriosis probably improves pregnancy: the odds of viable intrauterine pregnancy nearly doubled versus diagnostic laparoscopy alone (odds ratio 1.89, moderate-quality evidence). Whether it reduces pain, though, remains genuinely uncertain — the pain data were very low quality — and no trial reported live birth. lessons.title: The three faces of the disease — and why size doesn't equal pain
lessons.opening: Maybe someone once glanced at your scan and pronounced your case 'mild,' while your life kept shrinking around the pain. The word didn't match what you were living.
teaching:
Superficial peritoneal implants

The most common form of endometriosis — small patches of endometriotic tissue scattered across the peritoneum (the thin tissue that lines the pelvic cavity). Lesions can be red, dark, white, or non-pigmented depending on age and activity.

How it shows up: dysmenorrhea, deep dyspareunia, and chronic pelvic pain with often-normal-looking imaging. Transvaginal ultrasound does NOT reliably detect superficial peritoneal disease[5]Transvaginal ultrasound vs magnetic resonance imaging for diagnosing deep infiltrating endometriosis: systematic review and meta-analysis.Ultrasound Obstet Gynecol 2018 · PMID 29154402Transvaginal ultrasound matches MRI for detecting deep infiltrating endometriosis: both were about 85% sensitive and 95-96% specific for rectosigmoid disease, with similar performance at the uterosacral ligaments and rectovaginal septum — so either test can map deep disease before surgery. Meta-analysis of six studies (424 women) in which every patient underwent both tests with surgery as the reference standard; confidence intervals were wide and heterogeneity moderate to high, limiting precision.Read the study on PubMed →, which is one of the reasons a normal ultrasound does NOT rule out endometriosis.

Ovarian endometriomas (“chocolate cysts”)

Cysts on the ovary lined by endometriotic tissue and filled with old, dark blood — sometimes called “chocolate cysts” for their characteristic appearance. Highly visible on transvaginal ultrasound with the classic ground-glass echogenicity (sensitivity 83–93%, specificity 89–97%)[5]Transvaginal ultrasound vs magnetic resonance imaging for diagnosing deep infiltrating endometriosis: systematic review and meta-analysis.Ultrasound Obstet Gynecol 2018 · PMID 29154402Transvaginal ultrasound matches MRI for detecting deep infiltrating endometriosis: both were about 85% sensitive and 95-96% specific for rectosigmoid disease, with similar performance at the uterosacral ligaments and rectovaginal septum — so either test can map deep disease before surgery. Meta-analysis of six studies (424 women) in which every patient underwent both tests with surgery as the reference standard; confidence intervals were wide and heterogeneity moderate to high, limiting precision.Read the study on PubMed →.

Why they matter: endometriomas reduce ovarian reserve over time (which is why we check an AMH early), can rupture, and can become very large. The largest concern is their association with reduced fertility potential and with pelvic adhesion formation.

Deep infiltrating endometriosis (DIE)

Lesions that grow more than 5 mm beneath the peritoneal surface — into the bowel wall, the bladder wall, the rectovaginal septum, or the ligaments behind the uterus (the uterosacral ligaments). Causes the most severe symptoms and usually requires detailed MRI mapping before any surgery is planned.

How it shows up: pain with bowel movements (dyschezia), pain with urination, deep dyspareunia in specific positions, cyclic rectal bleeding, cyclic hematuria, or a fixed retroverted uterus on exam.

One thing that surprises most people: the severity of symptoms does not match the visible amount of disease. A woman with a tiny patch of superficial endometriosis can have debilitating pain, while a woman with a 6 cm endometrioma may have almost none[1]Diagnosis of Endometriosis.Obstet Gynecol 2026 · PMID 41712950Clinical diagnosis is enough to start treating endometriosis - laparoscopy is no longer required first. The guideline grades its recommendations for the clinical, imaging and surgical evaluation of endometriosis by strength and evidence quality, and adds ungraded good-practice points where evidence is inadequate or missing. The recommendations apply to adolescents as well as adults unless stated otherwise, though the adolescent guidance leans on data extrapolated from adults and on expert consensus (ACOG clinical practice guideline).Read the study on PubMed →.

lessons.title: 190 million strong: the numbers behind you
lessons.opening: You've heard 'lots of women have bad periods' so many times it started to sound like a verdict. What no one told you is how many women are quietly carrying the same unanswered question.
teaching:
How common it is

6–10% of reproductive-age women — roughly 190 million worldwide[13]ESHRE guideline: endometriosis.Hum Reprod Open 2022 · PMID 35350465Laparoscopy and histology are no longer the unchallenged gold standard for diagnosing endometriosis — one of the notable shifts in this guideline's 109 recommendations spanning diagnosis, pain and infertility treatment, recurrence, asymptomatic and extrapelvic disease, adolescents, postmenopausal patients, prevention, and cancer association. Developed by ESHRE from evidence through December 2020, it flags five topics where recommendations changed enough to alter practice, while conceding the evidence stays too scarce for firm answers on several questions.Read the study on PubMed →.

The numbers, from the national guideline

Endometriosis is endometrial-like tissue growing where it does not belong — most often on the ovaries, the pelvic sidewall, the uterosacral ligaments, the bowel, the bladder, the ureter, and (less commonly) the diaphragm. Per ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline No. 11, it affects 6–10% of reproductive-age women and rises to roughly 38% (range 20–50%) of women evaluated for infertility; the same guideline reports that having a first-degree relative with endometriosis carries a 7–10× increased risk of developing it yourself.
lessons.reflection: What would it change for you to sit in a waiting room knowing the women beside you might be carrying the same story?

action.text: If your symptoms have been brushed off as too common to matter, bring this lesson's numbers to your visit in writing — figures are harder to dismiss than adjectives.
action.question: Given how common endometriosis is, what would it take to evaluate me for it formally instead of assuming my pain is normal?

lessons.title: Four overlapping pain sources, all real, all physical
lessons.opening: You've tried explaining that the pain isn't one thing — it moves, it changes character, it shows up on days it has no business showing up. Mostly, you've watched that explanation get flattened into a single word: cramps.
teaching:
Why it hurts

One of the reasons endometriosis is so often under-treated is that pain in this condition is never coming from just one place. Treating only the lesions — with hormones or even with surgery — leaves the other three layers untreated, which is why so many women continue to hurt after “the surgery went well.”

From the clinic counseling script, verbatim

In endometriosis, pain comes from at least four overlapping sources simultaneously: the lesions themselves releasing inflammatory chemicals like prostaglandins and cytokines; the nerves around the lesions, which become abnormally sensitive over time; the pelvic-floor muscles, which develop trigger points and tightness as a guarding response; and the fascia and ligaments — especially the broad ligament and uterosacral ligaments — which can become restricted by adhesions and inflammation. Hormonal therapy reduces the activity of the lesions but does not directly address the muscle tightness, the fascial restriction, or the sensitized pain pathways — which is why some women continue to have pain even after good hormonal control or after excision surgery.

Layer one — the lesions themselves

Each endometriotic implant releases prostaglandins (especially PGE2 and PGF2α) and pro-inflammatory cytokines — the same chemical signals that drive ordinary menstrual cramps, only produced constantly and locally rather than cyclically. This is what produces the classic cyclic pain pattern early in the disease.

What targets this layer: NSAIDs (which inhibit prostaglandin synthesis directly) and continuous hormonal contraception (which suppresses ovulation and the cyclic hormonal trigger that drives lesion activity). The Cochrane evidence base supports the role of laparoscopic excision for patients for whom medication alone hasn’t been enough[2]Laparoscopic surgery for endometriosis.Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020 · PMID 33095458Laparoscopic treatment of endometriosis probably improves pregnancy: the odds of viable intrauterine pregnancy nearly doubled versus diagnostic laparoscopy alone (odds ratio 1.89, moderate-quality evidence). Whether it reduces pain, though, remains genuinely uncertain — the pain data were very low quality — and no trial reported live birth. Cochrane review of 14 randomized trials with 1,563 women; ablation versus excision showed no detectable difference, and adverse-event data were too sparse to judge safety.Read the study on PubMed →.
lessons.reflection: If you mapped your pain honestly — where it lives, when it visits, what it interrupts — what would that map show that your chart doesn't?

options.text: Mast cell activation is what drives endometriosis pain — endo is basically an allergy-type condition, so targeting mast cells is the answer.
Endometriosis pain comes from the lesions alone, so once the lesions are treated there is no other physical source left.

Partially supported — mechanism dense; clinical translation pending. Mast-cell activation is mechanistically established as a contributor, but no clinical RCT evidence exists for any mast-cell-targeted therapy in endometriosis. The bench is convincing; the bedside trials don't exist yet.

check.explanation: The reasonable part is that the bench science is genuinely strong — mast-cell activation is mechanistically established as a contributor to endometriosis pelvic pain. What's missing is the bedside: no clinical RCT evidence exists for any mast-cell-targeted therapy in endometriosis, so the mechanism is convincing but the clinical translation is still pending — and pain in this condition comes from overlapping sources, not one pathway.

action.text: Bring the four-layer map to your next visit so an untreated layer can't quietly stay off the agenda.
action.question: Which of the four pain sources — lesions, sensitized nerves, pelvic-floor muscles, fascia and ligaments — has my care plan addressed so far, and which haven't we touched?

lessons.title: It is not in your head (but your nervous system is involved)
lessons.opening: At some point, after enough shrugs and normal results, you started asking yourself the cruelest question of all: what if it really is just me?
teaching:
“I think the pain is in my head. Could that be it?”

It is not “in your head,” but the nervous system is part of the story — in a real, physical way. Long-standing pain rewires the spinal cord and brain to amplify pain signals (central sensitization)[7]Chronic Pelvic Pain: ACOG Practice Bulletin Summary, Number 218.Obstet Gynecol 2020 · PMID 32080045Chronic pelvic pain that is not fully explained by gynecologic, urologic, or gastrointestinal pathology still belongs in the gynecologist's scope — managed with longer visits (using appropriate coding modifiers) and a multidisciplinary team built within the practice or through facilitated referral. Where direct evidence is limited, recommendations are extrapolated from other chronic pain conditions; endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids, and vulvar disorders are covered in separate ACOG documents (Practice Bulletin 218 summary).Read the study on PubMed →. That is why some women continue to have pain even after the visible lesions are gone, and why a multi-modal approach — hormones plus pelvic-floor PT plus OMT plus, sometimes, neuromodulators like low-dose amitriptyline or gabapentin — is more effective than any single therapy alone. Acknowledging the nervous-system component is not dismissing your pain. It is the opposite: it is taking it seriously enough to actually address it.

Sensitized nerves — peripheral and central sensitization

Nerves around long-standing endometriotic lesions become abnormally amplified. This happens in two stages. First, peripheral sensitization: the nerve endings near the lesions develop a lower firing threshold, so even normal stimuli (a bowel movement, ovulation, intercourse) trigger pain signals. Second, central sensitization: the spinal cord and brain pathways that process those signals also amplify, so the pain becomes generalized, persistent, and disproportionate to the visible disease.

Why this matters clinically: once central sensitization is established, removing the lesions surgically does NOT automatically stop the pain — the nervous system has been “re-wired.” This is why women who wait years for diagnosis often have pain that persists even after excision.

options.text: If your pain continues after the lesions were treated, it must be in your head.

action.question: Could central sensitization be part of my ongoing pain, and is anything in my plan addressing it — not just the lesions?

lessons.title: The symptom pattern that should put endo on the table
lessons.opening: You could recite your symptoms in your sleep by now — you've repeated them in that many exam rooms. What you haven't been handed is the pattern they add up to.

The symptom pattern

lessons.title: You don't need surgery to be diagnosed — and where surgery still fits
lessons.opening: Somewhere along the way you absorbed the idea that nothing counts until a surgeon has seen it — that your account of your own body is provisional until an operation says otherwise.
teaching:
You do not need surgery to be diagnosed

For decades, a definitive diagnosis required laparoscopic surgery. That standard has changed. Where surgery still fits

The national guideline is clear: definitive diagnosis only comes from histology of lesions removed at surgery. Imaging and serum markers have not been able to replace diagnostic laparoscopy. lessons.title: What ultrasound and MRI can and can't see
lessons.opening: You've kept a mental list of the scans that came back 'fine' — and of the faces that looked at you differently once they did.
teaching:
Compartment-based transvaginal ultrasound

Performed in office by the same clinician who knows the history — not outsourced to a general sonographer whose protocol isn’t set up to look for endometriosis. We use the compartment-based protocol recommended by current systematic reviews and the SRU/IDEA consensus: anterior compartment (the space between bladder and uterus, bladder wall), middle compartment (uterus including signs of adenomyosis, ovaries including endometriomas, fallopian tubes), posterior compartment (uterosacral ligaments, rectovaginal septum, the cul-de-sac, the rectosigmoid). The uterine sliding sign assesses for cul-de-sac obliteration — whether the back of the uterus moves freely against the rectum, or whether scarring has glued them together. Added selectively, not as a screening test. We order MRI when the ultrasound shows signs of deep disease (fixed retroverted uterus, obliterated cul-de-sac, complex endometriomas, suggestion of rectovaginal-septum involvement), when symptoms suggest bowel or bladder infiltration (cyclic dyschezia, hematuria, severe deep dyspareunia), or when surgical planning would benefit from a detailed map of the structures involved. lessons.title: The five-step evaluation (including the exam most clinics skip)
lessons.opening: You've had appointments that were over in eight minutes, where you left holding a prescription and none of your questions. Part of you stopped expecting to be examined thoroughly at all.
teaching:
Step 1 — Detailed pain history & functional impact

The single most diagnostically valuable part of the visit. We document the pain character (cramping, sharp, aching, burning), the cyclicality (with periods only, mid-cycle, continuous), the location and radiation, a 0–10 numeric severity score (the VAS), the timeline of progression, and the concrete functional impact — work or school days missed, activities you have given up, the effect on relationships, the effect on sleep and mood. The baseline pain diary you start at this visit becomes the objective measurement against which every future treatment response is judged. Without a baseline number, you cannot tell whether you are 30% better or 5% better at the 3-month mark. We also assess all classic endometriosis symptoms in detail: dysmenorrhea (OR 8.1), deep dyspareunia (OR 6.0), dyschezia, dysuria, non-menstrual pelvic pain, and any prior treatment trials so we don’t repeat regimens that already failed.

Step 4 — Targeted bloodwork

What we order, and why:

  • CBC with iron studies (including ferritin): screen for anemia from heavy menstrual bleeding. Ferritin under 30 indicates iron deficiency; under 15 indicates depleted stores.
  • Pregnancy test (β-hCG): mandatory before any hormonal therapy is started.
  • CA-125: ordered only when an endometrioma is present, as a baseline for future surveillance. ACOG explicitly recommends against using CA-125 as a diagnostic test for endometriosis — it lacks the sensitivity and specificity[1]Diagnosis of Endometriosis.Obstet Gynecol 2026 · PMID 41712950Clinical diagnosis is enough to start treating endometriosis - laparoscopy is no longer required first. The guideline grades its recommendations for the clinical, imaging and surgical evaluation of endometriosis by strength and evidence quality, and adds ungraded good-practice points where evidence is inadequate or missing. The recommendations apply to adolescents as well as adults unless stated otherwise, though the adolescent guidance leans on data extrapolated from adults and on expert consensus (ACOG clinical practice guideline).Read the study on PubMed →.
  • AMH (anti-Müllerian hormone): ordered when reproductive timing is a consideration or when an endometrioma exists that may require cystectomy. Drawn independent of cycle day.
  • TSH: rule out thyroid dysfunction as a contributor to menstrual irregularity.
  • UA, GC/CT NAAT, vaginal swab: rule out infection, interstitial cystitis, and PID as differential diagnoses.

Step 5 — Pelvic floor examination

An assessment most clinics skip. Because 50–80% of women with endometriosis or chronic pelvic pain have a coexisting pelvic floor muscle component[7]Chronic Pelvic Pain: ACOG Practice Bulletin Summary, Number 218.Obstet Gynecol 2020 · PMID 32080045Chronic pelvic pain that is not fully explained by gynecologic, urologic, or gastrointestinal pathology still belongs in the gynecologist's scope — managed with longer visits (using appropriate coding modifiers) and a multidisciplinary team built within the practice or through facilitated referral. Where direct evidence is limited, recommendations are extrapolated from other chronic pain conditions; endometriosis, adenomyosis, fibroids, and vulvar disorders are covered in separate ACOG documents (Practice Bulletin 218 summary).Read the study on PubMed →[12]Randomized multicenter clinical trial of myofascial physical therapy in women with interstitial cystitis/painful bladder syndrome and pelvic floor tenderness.J Urol 2012 · PMID 22503015Pelvic floor myofascial physical therapy beats generic massage for interstitial cystitis/painful bladder syndrome with pelvic floor tenderness: 59% of women responded versus 26% with global therapeutic massage in this 11-center randomized trial of 81 women within three years of symptom onset. Pain was the most common adverse event at similar rates in both arms, and no serious adverse events occurred — supporting targeted myofascial therapy for this phenotype.Read the study on PubMed →, missing this is the single biggest reason women have pain after “a successful endometriosis surgery.” We palpate the levator ani group, the obturator internus, the piriformis, and the iliopsoas — looking for trigger points, tight bands, and an inability to relax voluntarily. We also assess the abdominal wall (Carnett-positive trigger points). If pelvic-floor dysfunction is present, pelvic-floor physical therapy is started in parallel with whatever hormonal or surgical plan we make for the lesions themselves — they are two separate problems and they need two separate treatment streams.

action.text: Start a baseline pain diary now — character, timing, location, radiation — and ask for the assessment most clinics skip, so future treatment response gets judged in numbers.
action.question: Will my evaluation include a pelvic-floor muscle examination — and if not, can we add one?

modules.title: Your Treatment Options: The Honest Menu
modules.what: The full menu of paths — watchful waiting, medication, surgery, and the hands-on adjuncts — with what counts as a fair trial of each.

lessons.title: Three honest paths: expectant, medical, surgical
lessons.opening: You’ve collected treatment suggestions the way other people collect receipts — a pill from one doctor, a shrug from another, a surgery pamphlet from a third — without anyone laying the whole menu on the table at once.
teaching:
Path 1 — Watchful waiting + NSAIDs

An option the national guideline acknowledges when symptoms are mild and infertility is not a near-term goal. Always paired with structured tracking.

  • Best for mild pain, no near-term fertility plan, no organ involvement on imaging.
  • NSAIDs are first-line analgesia per the national guideline.
  • Track symptoms with a pain-and-bleeding diary so a change is recognized early.
  • Pelvic floor physical therapy is under-used and helps the musculoskeletal contributors.

Recurrence is real even when nothing is done; the national guideline explicitly notes high baseline recurrence rates.

Path 2 — Hormonal suppression

Medications quiet symptoms but do not erase disease. The national guideline ranks birth-control pills as first-line for painful periods and reserves GnRH agonists for cases that resist other treatment.

  • Combined oral contraceptives — first-line for dysmenorrhea; continuous use often performs better than cyclic.
  • Oral norethindrone or depot medroxyprogesterone — Level B evidence; equivalent to more expensive regimens.
  • Long-term OC use reduces endometrioma recurrence and dysmenorrhea recurrence (Level B).
  • A time-limited empiric GnRH-agonist trial after first-line therapy fails is supported by the national guideline (Level B); add-back therapy supports continued use.
  • Elagolix (oral GnRH antagonist) — newer option for moderate-to-severe pain per the NEJM randomized trials (Taylor et al.).
  • Suppression is NOT a fertility treatment (Level A — explicitly).

When the medication stops, pain often returns. Plan accordingly.

Path 3 — Laparoscopic / robotic excision

The most definitive way to confirm the diagnosis and remove disease. Supported by the national guideline for refractory pain, infertility, and endometriomas.
lessons.reflection: If someone asked you to name your first priority right now — quieting the pain, protecting your fertility, or simply understanding the options — which answer would come out, and has your care ever started from it?

options.text: Plausible biology, but no endometriosis RCT: GLP-1 receptor agonists have biologically plausible routes to affect lesion biology, yet no randomized clinical trial has been conducted in endometriosis patients and no society recommends them for endometriosis — any lesion-burden effect is a hypothetical secondary benefit.
Ozempic-type drugs (GLP-1 receptor agonists like semaglutide and tirzepatide) shrink endometriosis lesions.
Hormonal suppression doubles as a fertility treatment — staying on the pill now will improve your chances of conceiving later.

check.explanation: It sounds believable because GLP-1 drugs really are reshaping treatment across metabolic and inflammatory conditions, and they have biologically plausible routes to affect lesion biology. But no randomized clinical trial has been conducted in endometriosis patients, and no society recommends them for endometriosis — any lesion-burden effect is a hypothetical secondary benefit, not a treatment path.

action.text: Bring the three-path menu to your next visit so the conversation starts from your goals instead of a default prescription.
action.question: Which of the three paths — expectant with structured symptom tracking, medical, or surgical — fits my goals right now, and what would move me from one to another?

lessons.title: The four-rung ladder: fair trials, timelines, and when to escalate
lessons.opening: You may have quit a medication at week six because nobody told you what a fair trial was — or stayed on one for two years because nobody named the moment to stop waiting.
teaching:
How the ladder works

Endometriosis is a chronic, estrogen-dependent condition. Most treatments work by reducing or eliminating monthly cycles, which both calms current symptoms and slows disease progression[2]Laparoscopic surgery for endometriosis.Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020 · PMID 33095458Laparoscopic treatment of endometriosis probably improves pregnancy: the odds of viable intrauterine pregnancy nearly doubled versus diagnostic laparoscopy alone (odds ratio 1.89, moderate-quality evidence). Whether it reduces pain, though, remains genuinely uncertain — the pain data were very low quality — and no trial reported live birth. Cochrane review of 14 randomized trials with 1,563 women; ablation versus excision showed no detectable difference, and adverse-event data were too sparse to judge safety.Read the study on PubMed →[6]Endometriosis recurrence following post-operative hormonal suppression: a systematic review and meta-analysis.Hum Reprod Update 2021 · PMID 33020832Starting hormonal suppression within six weeks after endometriosis surgery cut disease recurrence by more than half (relative risk 0.41) and lowered pain scores versus expectant management or placebo. Meta-analysis of 17 studies with 2,137 patients covering combined contraceptives, progestins, the levonorgestrel IUD, and GnRH agonists — the effect held across subgroups and high-quality studies, so agent choice can be individualized. Recommended for women not seeking immediate pregnancy; between-study heterogeneity was substantial.Read the study on PubMed →. We move up the ladder one step at a time, judging each on response over 3–6 months.

Evidence on live birth, miscarriage, adverse events, and all other interventions was insufficient, and the authors' chief message is that trials comparing IVF and intrauterine insemination against other treatments are still badly needed.Read the study on PubMed →.

The first rung, and what a fair trial looks like

First-line for almost everyone: NSAIDs + continuous hormonal contraception. NSAIDs taken pre-emptively 1–2 days before period (more effective than waiting until pain starts). Cochrane review of 14 randomized trials with 1,563 women; ablation versus excision showed no detectable difference, and adverse-event data were too sparse to judge safety.Read the study on PubMed →.

If first-line is not working at 3 months, we escalate[2]Laparoscopic surgery for endometriosis.Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020 · PMID 33095458Laparoscopic treatment of endometriosis probably improves pregnancy: the odds of viable intrauterine pregnancy nearly doubled versus diagnostic laparoscopy alone (odds ratio 1.89, moderate-quality evidence). If medical therapy doesn’t work

We escalate. The standard step-up: first-line OCP or NSAIDs → second-line progestin-only or LNG-IUD → third-line GnRH antagonist with add-back hormones. If you have given two adequate trials (3–6 months each) and still have functional pain, that is when surgical evaluation moves to the front of the conversation.

Surgery for endometriosis is laparoscopic excision — cutting out the lesions, freeing adhesions, treating endometriomas by cystectomy (not just draining them). Whether it reduces pain, though, remains genuinely uncertain — the pain data were very low quality — and no trial reported live birth. Cochrane review of 14 randomized trials with 1,563 women; ablation versus excision showed no detectable difference, and adverse-event data were too sparse to judge safety.Read the study on PubMed →. lessons.reflection: Looking back at each treatment you’ve tried, which ones actually got a fair trial — and which ones ended in silence, side effects, or giving up?

options.text: Surgery is the only treatment that really works — medications just delay the inevitable.
The ladder is really a stalling tactic — doctors make you fail three medications because insurance requires it, not because the steps can work.

Most women respond without an operation: 60–80% have meaningful pain relief on first-line medical therapy, and treatment moves up a ladder one step at a time — NSAIDs plus continuous hormonal contraception, then progestin-only therapy or the LNG-IUD, then a GnRH antagonist with add-back — with surgery reserved for failed medical therapy, fertility goals, or an endometrioma threatening the ovary.

check.explanation: The belief is understandable — when pain keeps coming back on medication after medication, surgery starts to look like the only real exit. But 60–80% of women have meaningful pain relief on first-line medical therapy, and treatment moves up a ladder one step at a time — NSAIDs plus continuous hormonal contraception, then progestin-only therapy or the LNG-IUD, then a GnRH antagonist with add-back — with surgery reserved for failed medical therapy, fertility goals, or an endometrioma threatening the ovary. Most women don’t end up needing surgery at all.

action.text: Put a three-month checkpoint on your calendar for the step you’re on, so escalation is a scheduled decision rather than a moment of exhaustion.
action.question: Have I given my current step a fair trial yet — and if it isn’t working at the three-month mark, what is the next rung for me?

lessons.title: What hormonal therapy does (and doesn’t do)
lessons.opening: There’s a version of hope you’ve probably been sold — take this and it will all be over — and a quieter truth nobody quite said out loud at the pharmacy counter.
teaching:
Will hormonal therapy cure it?

No. Hormonal therapy is suppressive — it controls symptoms and slows progression but does not eliminate the disease. The published evidence shows medical suppressive therapy improves pain in most women, but recurrence rates are high after the medication is stopped[6]Endometriosis recurrence following post-operative hormonal suppression: a systematic review and meta-analysis.Hum Reprod Update 2021 · PMID 33020832Starting hormonal suppression within six weeks after endometriosis surgery cut disease recurrence by more than half (relative risk 0.41) and lowered pain scores versus expectant management or placebo. Meta-analysis of 17 studies with 2,137 patients covering combined contraceptives, progestins, the levonorgestrel IUD, and GnRH agonists — the effect held across subgroups and high-quality studies, so agent choice can be individualized. Recommended for women not seeking immediate pregnancy; between-study heterogeneity was substantial.Read the study on PubMed →. The honest framing is: we are managing a chronic condition, not curing it.

For most women, that management continues until menopause or until they want to try to conceive. Step therapy gives us multiple options to rotate through, so that a side effect on one medication doesn’t end the conversation.

If hormones don’t cure it, why bother?

Three reasons. First, 60–80% of women have meaningful pain relief on first-line therapy[2]Laparoscopic surgery for endometriosis.Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020 · PMID 33095458Laparoscopic treatment of endometriosis probably improves pregnancy: the odds of viable intrauterine pregnancy nearly doubled versus diagnostic laparoscopy alone (odds ratio 1.89, moderate-quality evidence). Whether it reduces pain, though, remains genuinely uncertain — the pain data were very low quality — and no trial reported live birth. Cochrane review of 14 randomized trials with 1,563 women; ablation versus excision showed no detectable difference, and adverse-event data were too sparse to judge safety.Read the study on PubMed → — without surgery, recovery time, or surgical complications. lessons.title: What Level A evidence actually says (and how to read a claim)
lessons.opening: You’ve been down the 2 a.m. rabbit hole — a forum thread, a miracle story, a video swearing by something no doctor has mentioned to you — and surfaced less certain than when you started.
teaching:
What the national guideline says

These are the Level A (good and consistent scientific evidence) recommendations from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists — the national guideline body for this specialty — that shape every conversation about diagnosis, medical therapy, and surgery for endometriosis. They are the standard of care, not opinion.

  • Ultrasound first — Transvaginal ultrasound is the imaging modality of choice for assessing the presence of endometriosis. ACOG Guideline No. 11 · Level A
  • Excision beats ablation — For endometriomas, cutting the cyst out is superior to simple drainage and burning of the cyst wall. ACOG Guideline No. 11 · Level A
  • Surgery helps fertility — Surgical management of endometriosis-related infertility improves pregnancy rates; magnitude unclear. ACOG Guideline No. 11 · Level A
  • Suppression won’t restore fertility — Birth-control pills and GnRH agonists quiet pain but are ineffective for endometriosis-associated infertility. ACOG Guideline No. 11 · Level A
  • Medication eases pain — Medical suppressive therapy improves pain — but recurrence rates are high after stopping. ACOG Guideline No. 11 · Level A
  • Surgery eases pain — Significant short-term improvement in pain after conservative surgical excision — recurrence still happens. ACOG Guideline No. 11 · Level A

The evidence underneath the claims

  • Diagnosis of Endometriosis, Obstet Gynecol 2026 — ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline — Diagnosis of Endometriosis. Affirms clinical diagnosis as sufficient: laparoscopy is no longer required to start treatment. PMID 41712950
  • Bafort et al., Laparoscopic surgery for endometriosis, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020 — Cochrane systematic review — laparoscopic excision provides overall pain relief versus no treatment or diagnostic-only laparoscopy in endometriosis. PMID 33095458
  • Zakhari et al., Endometriosis recurrence following post-operative hormonal suppression: a systematic review and meta-analysis, Hum Reprod Update 2021 — post-operative hormonal suppression significantly reduces endometriosis and pain recurrence after excision. PMID 33020832
  • Hodgson et al., Interventions for endometriosis-related infertility: a systematic review and network meta-analysis, Fertil Steril 2020 — network meta-analysis: surgery for endometriosis improves clinical pregnancy rates compared with the wait-and-monitor approach. PMID 32106991
lessons.reflection: Which treatment claim from your own late-night searching would you most want to hold up to the light of the randomized-trial question?

options.text: Over-the-counter antihistamines like famotidine (Pepcid) and cetirizine (Zyrtec) are a proven treatment for endometriosis pain.
A convincing mechanism is enough — when the bench science is solid, a randomized trial is a formality that just hasn’t been scheduled yet.

The mechanism is real, but the trial is not: the mast-cell/histamine pathway is well-documented at the bench, yet no randomized trial of H1 or H2 antihistamines in endometriosis pain has been published and no major society includes them in any practice guideline — for overlapping mast-cell/allergic phenotypes an antihistamine trial is a reasonable add-on to suppressive therapy, as add-on, not replacement.

check.explanation: It sounds credible because the mast-cell/histamine pathway really is well-documented at the bench — the mechanism is real. But no randomized trial of H1 or H2 antihistamines in endometriosis pain has been published, and no major society includes them in any practice guideline. For overlapping mast-cell/allergic phenotypes an antihistamine trial can be a reasonable add-on to suppressive therapy — as add-on, not replacement.

action.text: Keep this question saved in your phone for anything you see recommended online, so visit time goes to weighing evidence rather than untangling headlines.
action.question: Is there a randomized trial behind this in endometriosis patients, or bench evidence only — and is it in any society guideline?

modules.title: Surgery Done Right: Excision and Choosing Your Surgeon
modules.what: What excellent excision surgery looks like, when it is the right call, and the questions that show whether a surgeon clears the bar.

lessons.title: Cutting vs burning: what Level A evidence says
lessons.opening: You’ve heard both phrases — “we’ll laser it” and “we’ll cut it out” — used as if they named the same operation, and no one paused to explain the difference.
teaching:
Cutting vs burning

Ablation burns the surface of the lesion away. Excision cuts the lesion out entirely, including the deeper tissue you can’t see from the surface. For ovarian endometriomas the published evidence is clear: excising the cyst wall (cystectomy) is superior to draining and ablating it — lower recurrence and better symptom relief[2]Laparoscopic surgery for endometriosis.Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020 · PMID 33095458Laparoscopic treatment of endometriosis probably improves pregnancy: the odds of viable intrauterine pregnancy nearly doubled versus diagnostic laparoscopy alone (odds ratio 1.89, moderate-quality evidence). Whether it reduces pain, though, remains genuinely uncertain — the pain data were very low quality — and no trial reported live birth. Cochrane review of 14 randomized trials with 1,563 women; ablation versus excision showed no detectable difference, and adverse-event data were too sparse to judge safety.Read the study on PubMed →. For peritoneal disease, excision is also preferred when technically feasible. Excision is performed laparoscopically as the default approach.

What the national guideline anchors

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists Clinical Practice Guideline No. 11 is the current authoritative U.S. guidance on managing the disease. Two of its Level A (good and consistent evidence) recommendations sit at the center of how this practice operates: (1) excision of an endometrioma is superior to simple drainage and ablation of the cyst wall, and (2) surgical management of endometriosis-related infertility does improve pregnancy rates. Together they explain why the operation here is always a true excision — cutting the lesion out at its root and sending every specimen to pathology — rather than a surface burn.

Why not just burn the lesions?

The national guideline calls this out as a Level A recommendation for endometriomas specifically: excision is superior to simple drainage and ablation of the cyst wall. Excision removes the disease at its root, lets pathology confirm the diagnosis, and produces measurably better outcomes than burning the surface.

lessons.title: What a laparoscopic excision involves — and its risks, quantified
lessons.opening: The operating room may live in your imagination as a blank: you go to sleep, something happens, you wake up different. The unknown middle can be its own kind of fear.
teaching:
What the operation involves

What “laparoscopic excision” means concretely: a same-day-discharge minimally-invasive procedure done through small ¼-inch incisions, under general anesthesia, with magnified high-definition visualization. Endometriotic lesions are cut out (excision) rather than burned (ablation). Adhesions are released. Endometriomas are cystectomized — the cyst wall is peeled away and removed in its entirety. If deep disease involves the bowel, bladder, or ureter, a multidisciplinary team (colorectal, urology) is scrubbed in based on the pre-operative MRI map.

Risks reviewed: bleeding (typically minimal, occasionally requires transfusion in extensive cases), infection (less than 1%), injury to nearby organs — bowel, bladder, ureter, blood vessels (each less than 1% with experienced CBG/MIGS hands), formation of new adhesions (mitigated by careful technique and adhesion barriers), reduction in ovarian reserve when operating on the ovary itself (mitigated by careful preservation of normal ovarian cortex), risks of general anesthesia. Same-day discharge for most cases. Return to office work approximately 1 week; return to heavy physical work or sport approximately 2–4 weeks.

When deep disease is on the map

Surgical considerations: deep disease often requires a multidisciplinary team — colorectal surgery for bowel involvement, urology for ureter or bladder involvement. The MRI map drives the decision about which specialists are scrubbed into the case. Is surgery safe?

lessons.title: What excellence looks like: ICG, cystoscopy, pathology, the right team
lessons.opening: You’ve been told to “find a good surgeon” as though excellence were something you could sense in a waiting room, with no checklist to make it visible.
teaching:
The ICG refinement

The added refinement is indocyanine green (ICG) fluorescence imaging. ICG is a contrast agent that lights up fibrosis and inflammation under near-infrared light, so lesions that look normal under standard white light can reveal themselves. That refinement is grounded in this practice’s own published research: a retrospective cohort study of ICG in the detection of fibrosis and inflammatory changes related to endometriosis (Mabini & Tam, CAOG 91st Annual Meeting, 2024, awarded the George W. Morley Memorial Paper Award). The published work supports ICG as an intraoperative detection aid in advanced disease and deep infiltrating endometriosis, helping the surgeon find disease so it can be excised.

What is ICG and why use it?

Indocyanine green is a contrast dye used safely in surgery for decades. Under near-infrared light it highlights fibrotic and inflammatory tissue — exactly the territory where endometriosis hides under normal light. Adding ICG to the standard guideline-recommended laparoscopic approach is a detection aid: in this practice’s published cohort study (Mabini & Tam, CAOG 2024), it helped identify fibrosis and inflammatory changes related to endometriosis so that disease could be found and excised.

Markers of a complete operation

  • Excision of every visible (and ICG-fluorescent) lesion — superior to ablation per the national guideline (Level A).
  • Endometrioma cystectomy with ovarian-tissue preservation — excision > drainage + ablation per the national guideline (Level A).
  • Ureterolysis and careful bowel and rectosigmoid dissection when DIE is present, in the same operation; for the rare case that needs full-thickness bowel or bladder resection, colorectal surgery or urology colleagues operate alongside.
  • Improves pregnancy rates for endometriosis-related infertility per the national guideline (Level A; magnitude unclear).
  • Same-day discharge in 90.4% of minimally invasive fellowship cases; zero conversions to open surgery.
  • Even after definitive surgery (hysterectomy + BSO), the national guideline notes that disease can persist or recur; no operation removes that risk entirely.

Definitive diagnosis still requires histology of the excised tissue — every specimen is sent to pathology.

lessons.title: Getting ready: goals, meds, and ERAS optimization
lessons.opening: You've been handed a surgery date, and suddenly your kitchen counter is a pharmacy inventory you're not sure how to explain. The pre-op packet reads like it was written for someone calmer than you feel right now.
teaching:
Before surgery

Detailed history, exam, and transvaginal ultrasound as the guideline-recommended imaging baseline; pelvic MRI added when DIE is suspected. Pre-op covers your goals (pain vs. fertility vs. both), GLP-1 medication timing (Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro held per anesthesia protocol), blood thinners, hormone therapy, and ERAS optimization (anemia, nutrition, smoking).

lessons.title: What happens on the day of surgery
lessons.opening: You've pictured the morning a hundred times — the waiting room, the gown, the moment they wheel you back. It's the hours you won't remember that occupy you the most.
teaching:
Day of surgery

General anesthesia. Three to five small (5–12 mm) abdominal incisions. ICG injection where indicated. Every identified lesion is excised (not burned) to negative margins. A cystoscopy at the end confirms the ureters are intact. Most patients go home the same day.

First 2 weeks

Soreness rather than sharp pain. Alternating ibuprofen and acetaminophen handles most postoperative pain. Walking begins day one. No heavy lifting (>10 lb), no intercourse, no tampons for 2 weeks. Mild CO₂-related bloating resolves in 24–72 hours.

Return to activity

Same-day discharge for most cases. Return to office work approximately 1 week; return to heavy physical work or sport approximately 2–4 weeks.

lessons.title: When to call now, not at your next visit
lessons.opening: It's the middle of the night and something doesn't feel right — and you're doing the familiar math of not wanting to overreact against not wanting to wait too long. You've talked yourself out of calling before.
teaching:
When to call urgently

Call the office or seek care now if you have:

  • Sudden, severe one-sided pelvic pain — especially with nausea or vomiting (possible ovarian torsion)
  • Pain that prescribed medications are no longer touching
  • Bleeding heavy enough to soak through a pad or tampon every hour for two consecutive hours
  • Fever above 101°F with pelvic pain
  • New bowel symptoms — rectal bleeding, severe constipation, or pain with bowel movements that wasn’t there before
  • New urinary symptoms — blood in the urine, inability to fully empty the bladder
  • Pain so severe you cannot work, sleep, or function
  • If you suspect you are pregnant and you are on hormonal therapy

Only heavy bleeding truly counts as urgent — pain, fever, and new bowel or bladder symptoms can wait for the scheduled follow-up.

Some symptoms should not wait: sudden severe one-sided pelvic pain (especially with nausea/vomiting — possible torsion), fever above 101°F with pelvic pain, bleeding soaking a pad or tampon every hour for two consecutive hours, pain your prescribed medications no longer touch, new bowel or urinary symptoms, or pain so severe you cannot function. Call or seek care now.

Call or seek care now.

Once the surgeon removes it, it's gone for good — there's no need for medication afterward.

check.explanation: The logic feels airtight: if the lesions were cut out, they should be gone. But some of it can come back. Recurrence is roughly 20-40% at five years without ongoing therapy — dropping to 8-15% with post-operative hormonal suppression (usually an LNG-IUD placed at surgery or continuous combined OCP, continued until menopause or until you want to conceive). Skipping post-op suppression is the most common reason for symptomatic recurrence.

action.text: Have the suppression conversation before surgery, not after — the recurrence plan works best when it exists before the operation does.
action.question: What is my post-op suppression plan — an LNG-IUD placed at the time of surgery, or a continuous combined pill — and how long does it continue?

lessons.title: Managing a chronic condition, not curing it
lessons.opening: Part of you is still waiting for the appointment where someone says the word 'cured.' Learning to plan around a condition instead of past it is its own kind of grief — and its own kind of steadiness.
teaching:
The honest framing is: we are managing a chronic condition, not curing it.

For most women, that management continues until menopause or until they want to try to conceive. Step therapy gives us multiple options to rotate through, so that a side effect on one medication doesn’t end the conversation.
lessons.reflection: What would change for you if you stopped measuring your progress against a finish line and started measuring it against how you're living now?

action.text: Ask about rotation options ahead of time, so one bad side effect changes the medication rather than derailing the whole plan.
action.question: If this medication gives me side effects, what are my rotation options — and what stays the same in the plan when we switch?

lessons.title: Fertility planning: early, honest, evidence-based
lessons.opening: Maybe children are the plan, maybe a question mark, maybe not for years — but every appointment seems to circle the topic without landing on it. You've held back from asking directly because of what the answer might be.
teaching:
Endometriosis affects fertility in roughly 30–50% of women who have it, and it is found in about 38% of women evaluated for infertility[3]Association of endometriosis and adenomyosis with pregnancy and infertility.Fertil Steril 2023 · PMID 36948440Endometriosis and adenomyosis both reduce pregnancy and live birth rates and increase miscarriage — with the larger effect from adenomyosis — and severe forms of either warrant high-risk obstetric care at tertiary centers. Deep infiltrating endometriosis raises risks of placenta previa, spontaneous hemoperitoneum in pregnancy, and cesarean surgical complications; adenomyosis is linked to preeclampsia, preterm delivery, hemorrhage, and growth restriction. Synthesis of recent meta-analyses, which were markedly heterogeneous, so caution applies.Read the study on PubMed →[4]Interventions for endometriosis-related infertility: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.Fertil Steril 2020 · PMID 32106991Laparoscopic surgery and GnRH agonist therapy each raised the odds of pregnancy roughly 1.6-1.7-fold versus placebo in endometriosis-related infertility — but that is nearly all this network meta-analysis of 26 randomized trials (2,245 women) could conclude. Evidence on live birth, miscarriage, adverse events, and all other interventions was insufficient, and the authors' chief message is that trials comparing IVF and intrauterine insemination against other treatments are still badly needed.Read the study on PubMed →. Most women with endometriosis still conceive without help — especially with early diagnosis — but for those who don’t, the issue is usually a combination of pelvic adhesions, ovarian-reserve impact from endometriomas, and the inflammatory pelvic environment.

If you have endometriosis and you are thinking about pregnancy: raise it at your visit early. Evidence on live birth, miscarriage, adverse events, and all other interventions was insufficient, and the authors' chief message is that trials comparing IVF and intrauterine insemination against other treatments are still badly needed.Read the study on PubMed →. We check AMH up front when there’s an endometrioma, so we know what we’re working with.

Will surgery hurt my fertility?

Done well, no. Endometrioma cystectomy carries a real risk of removing normal ovarian tissue, so technique matters; the national guideline notes excision is preferred over drainage+ablation even with that risk. For DIE, excision often improves spontaneous conception rates. Plan fertility timing BEFORE surgery, not after.

Can medication alone fix it if I want to get pregnant?

No — the national guideline is explicit (Level A): medical suppressive therapies such as oral contraceptives and GnRH agonists are ineffective for endometriosis-associated infertility. They quiet pain while you take them; they do not improve fertility. Surgery does improve pregnancy rates for infertility caused by endometriosis (Level A).

lessons.title: If pain comes back: the layers to re-check
lessons.opening: The pain you thought you'd closed the door on has started knocking again, and you're dreading the conversation where someone tells you the surgery 'worked.' You know your own baseline better than any chart does.
teaching:
If pain returns after surgery

What this means for you: if you have already had endometriosis surgery and pain has returned, the published evidence supports an osteopathic visceral-fascial protocol as a real additional treatment option — not instead of, but on top of, whatever hormonal treatment or further surgical treatment is appropriate.[11]Effects of osteopathic manipulative therapy on recurrent pelvic pain and dyspareunia in women after surgery for endometriosis: a retrospective study.Minerva Obstet Gynecol 2024 · PMID 37997320Pain that persists after endometriosis surgery may respond to osteopathic manipulative treatment: among 345 women operated for endometriosis, 28% had persistent pelvic pain and dyspareunia, and in 69 treated with myofascial and ligamentous techniques, pain scores fell sharply (mean 4 down to 0.2) starting from the first session. lessons.title: Staying connected: the long-term partnership
lessons.opening: You've read the modules, filled the margins with questions, and now there's just the phone call you've been putting off. Somewhere along the way you stopped expecting to be believed — and that's a hard habit to unlearn.
teaching:
Take the next step
